title: Living ashtpadi 21
hook: the vast and the quiet behind all things
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings

segments.voice: Yesterday, khel, and your line: the play begins. Did you make the first small start on something? Today we take the twenty-first ashtpadi, the stillness and the beginning, out into an ordinary morning. Day five hundred twenty-one.

Right before dawn, the sky does something odd. It isn't dark and it isn't light. It goes a deep, even gray-blue, and everything is very quiet: no birds yet, no traffic, the trees just shapes. Then, slowly, color comes in from one edge. First a line of pale yellow. Then pink. Then, all at once, it's morning, and the noise of the day begins. In a small way, the twenty-first ashtpadi plays out every dawn.
screen: `THE GRAY-BLUE BEFORE DAWN.` → `A LINE OF PALE YELLOW.` → `EVERY DAWN, THE ASHTPADI.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-first ashtpadi in brief. Before anything, the Formless One, nirankaar, rested in sunn, the deep stillness. There was no form, no grudge, no joy or sorrow, only the One. Then, by God's own will, the play began, and the world of forms spread out. Living that doesn't mean thinking about the beginning of the universe all day. It means remembering that the stillness didn't go anywhere. In Sikh teaching, the One who rested in sunn is the same One inside the play now, behind all things, the way the quiet gray sky is still there behind the colors of the sunrise. That's one reason Sikh practice values amrit vela, the hours before dawn. In Japji, Guru Nanak names that ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the greatness of the Name. It's the time of day that looks most like the ashtpadi: quiet first, then the world. Sitting with the Name then is a way of meeting the stillness before the noise begins, so that you can carry a little of it into the noise. And the noise is not the enemy. Sikh teaching has no quarrel with the busy day; the Gurus worked, farmed, traded and led. The point is that behind the busyness there's something vast and quiet that the busyness can't touch. Some mornings it's easy to sense, and some mornings it isn't. Sukhmani says it's there either way.
screen: `STILLNESS, THEN THE PLAY.` · `THE STILLNESS DIDN'T GO ANYWHERE.` · `AMRIT VELA: QUIET FIRST.` · `THE BUSY DAY IS NOT THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `BEHIND ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the dawn. If it's early, go to a window and watch the sky change. If it isn't, close your eyes and remember a dawn you've seen, or look at whatever sky is outside now. Watch slowly. Notice the quiet underneath the color, or underneath the light and noise of the day. Let your breath be as slow as the sky. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru, behind all things. The bell holds the time.
Nirankaar, the Formless One: the stillness nirankaar rested in before creation is still here, behind the play; amrit vela, before dawn, is a daily way to meet it.
Your line: behind all things. Tomorrow, try waking ten minutes earlier and sit before the day's noise starts. Tonight, set the alarm. Day five hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Sikh practice values rising at amrit vela, the hours before dawn that Japji names as the time to reflect on the Name, for quiet remembrance before the day begins.

myth: in Sikh teaching, the stillness ended when creation began
the One who rested in sunn is the same One behind all things now.
Japji names the ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the Name
living ashtpadi 21 means avoiding busy work
the Gurus worked, farmed and led; the quiet sits behind the busyness.

fork.setup: you want to meet the stillness of ashtpadi 21 each day. when does Sikh practice point to?
options: whenever there's nothing else to do.
fork.reveal: amrit vela. quiet first, then the world: the shape of the ashtpadi, every morning.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nirankaar, the Formless One, who rested in sunn before creation.

trapdoor: what you thought: living ashtpadi 21 means pondering the start of the universe.
what it means: remembering the vast quiet still behind all things, and meeting it before the day's noise.
what a scholar hears: Japji's pauri 4 names amrit vela as the time to reflect on the greatness of the Name, and the Sikh discipline of rising before dawn looks back to that line.
